author: Beulah Meriam K
title: Energizer Holdings ( ENR ) is one of the world’s top produce
text:
Energizer Holdings ( ENR ) is one of the world’s top producers of batteries and lighting products, also holding a respectable position in the automotive esthetics market. 
But, despite being in one of the hottest industries of the decade, Energizer Holdings has struggled to increase its sales over the last five years, while margins have remained extremely inconsistent. That, however, is merely the surface of the problem, as we’ll see. 
Operating margins are one of the metrics that I typically use to understand the strength of a company, and I’ve generally found that above-average companies will always have above-average margins, like Visa ( V ), Wal-Mart ( WMT ), Apple ( AAPL ) and Colgate-Palmolive ( CL ), to name just a few. That’s not to say there aren’t exceptions, such as Amazon ( AMZN ) or Tesla Motors ( TSLA ), but the rule of thumb here is that a company with a well-positioned offering and a solid management team will usually deliver operating margins above those of its industry peers.
ENR Operating Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts A lot of Energizer’s products are positioned in the premium segment, but the inconsistent operating margin shows that there is little to no effect due to that positioning. In turn, it reveals that competitive pressure is eating into what benefits Energizer should be enjoying at the bottom line.
“Energizer offers batteries using many technologies including lithium, alkaline, carbon zinc, nickel metal hydride, zinc air, and silver oxide. These products are sold under the Energizer and Eveready brands in the performance, premium and price segments and include primary, rechargeable, specialty and hearing aid products.” - Energizer Annual Report 2017 
Battery sales, which account for the bulk of Energizer’s revenues, have been flat over the last three years, staying around the $1.5 billion level. And this in a growing global battery market. In North America alone, the battery market’s revenues are projected to grow from the current $15 to $20 billion up to $25 to $30 billion in the next several years, as you can see in the chart below. 

Source: Grand View Research 
A lot of this growth is being fueled by an increased need for power storage solutions as the world moves toward renewable energy sources that can generally not be used at the point of production, such as geothermal, nuclear, hydro, wind and other forms. 

Source: International Energy Agency via Clean Technica 

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration 
It also will be ably supported by the global shift to EVs (electric vehicles) over traditional ICE (internal combustion engine) vehicles. 

Source: Economist 
As you can see, despite being in the business of power storage from 1893, Energizer has pretty much remained on the sidelines of major revolutions in the energy market. 
Even within its own niche, Energizer has allowed relative upstarts like Duracell and even Amazon to walk away with more than four times its own market share in the online space. 

Source: Seeking Alpha , Credit: 1010data 
While Amazon runs away with online battery sales thanks to a lower price positioning , Energizer is still struggling to bridge the gap with Duracell. As sales keeps transitioning to online channels, Amazon will continue to attract more volume, thus leaving Energizer with no choice but to take a hit on margins if it wants to increase market share. 
The biggest problem Energizer faces at this point is the slow growth in the household battery market. 
“ Packaged Facts projects that sales of household batteries will reach $4,750 million by the year 2020, up from $4,125 million in 2015. The CAGR for the period is a projected 2.9%. Three manufacturers dominate the U.S. market for household batteries: Berkshire Hathaway, which owns the Duracell brand; Energizer, maker of both Energizer and Eveready batteries; and Spectrum Brands, which makes Rayovac.” 
The problem for Energizer is two-fold. In the online arena the company already is pushed to fourth place, while in terms of shelf place it has to compete with Duracell. A saying about a rock and a hard place comes to mind when you look at its predicament. 
What that means is that revenue growth is going to be stable at best over the next several years. Any premium positioning advantage it enjoyed is now diluted by the need to fight for market share, which is definitely going to keep the company’s operating margins on their prolonged rollercoaster ride. 
One positive move is the decision to buy Spectrum, which was smart because it not only brings th e fourth-place bat tery brand into Energizer’s fold, but also adds a product at a lower price point. That gives it a little more scale and size with which to combat the growing dual-menace of Amazon and Duracell, not to mention Panasonic, which already has taken the lead role in the automobile electrification story. 

Source: Inside EVs 
Considering the current position that Energizer is in, I cannot see myself recommending the stock even though it’s trading near its fair price assuming a 3% growth rate projection over the next several years. 
The valuation might be reasonable, but it might not be reasonable to expect Energizer to make serious gains against AmazonBasics in the online space or Duracell in the physical retail world. Both of these are aggressive brands owned by deep-pocketed companies, and I just feel Energizer’s management hasn’t shown the kind of foresight or aggressiveness in claiming what could - and should - have been pole position, at the very least in household batteries.
